A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SimBa study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material relocated or renumbered in v2.

before.justification: v1 reports original reinforcement-learning experiments, architecture comparisons, ablations, and plasticity analyses, with learning curves and per-task results in the appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds component-removal experiments, extended training, correlation estimates, and expanded plasticity analyses.

M1.justification: SimBa retains RSNorm, pre-normalized residual feedforward blocks, post-layer normalization, and the same integrations into RL algorithms. The new component-removal variants are diagnostic ablations; the proposed architecture and training procedures are unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same DMC, MyoSuite, HumanoidBench, Craftax, and unsupervised Humanoid tasks. The added analyses reuse existing environments. Vision-based and multi-task RL appear only as future directions.

E2.justification: Section 7.1 and Figure 12 add RMSNorm as a sixth observation-normalization alternative. The existing off-policy benchmark comparators and architectural baselines remain; LayerNorm and BatchNorm are shortened names for retained comparators.

E3.justification: The original benchmark protocols remain unchanged. Appendix C.2 adds a five-million-step DMC-Hard follow-up alongside the retained one-million-step evaluation. Appendix D adds a correlation comparison across 12 architectures controlled to approximately 4.5 million parameters, with at most 1% variation.

E4.justification: Appendices C–E substantially expand the diagnostic evidence: individual component removals complement v1's component additions, extended training tests durability, and correlation analysis examines the simplicity–performance relationship. Plasticity analysis expands from the DMC-Hard architecture comparison to easier tasks and component ablations.

E5.justification: Appendix D introduces numerical correlation estimation, although Figure 17 says Spearman while its caption and discussion say Pearson. Figure 16 specifies five SimBa seeds and three seeds each for SAC and TD-MPC2, with 95% confidence intervals. Existing experiments retain their seed counts and uncertainty-reporting practices.

E6.justification: v2 adds RMSNorm scores, component-removal outcomes, five-million-step learning curves, expanded plasticity results, and correlations of 0.79 for architectures with RSNorm and 0.54 overall. Notably, removing RSNorm raises the simplicity score while reducing return. The original benchmark values in Tables 12–15 remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The Fourier complexity and simplicity-bias definitions, architectural equations, and plasticity metric formulas are retained, including Appendices A–B. The new correlation analysis introduces empirical evidence, without new mathematical definitions, assumptions, derivations, or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and concluding lessons retain the central claims: architectural simplicity bias enables parameter scaling, improves sample efficiency across RL algorithms, and provides competitive computational efficiency. The additional evidence does not redefine those contributions.

C2.justification: Appendices C.1 and D newly qualify the simplicity proxy: uniform input sampling may miss RSNorm's practical contribution. Appendix E adds task-dependent qualifications to the plasticity interpretation and discusses component interactions. Section 8 adds prospective applications to vision-based and multi-task RL.

D1.justification: Figure 5 now reports critic parameter counts instead of widths, and Appendix D documents approximate model sizes and the parameter-matching tolerance. The hyperparameter tables, hardware/software specifications, and code, Dockerfile, and raw-score access statements remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds Espeholt et al. (2018), acknowledging earlier residual architectures in RL, and Zhang and Sennrich (2019) for RMSNorm. The broader related-work discussion and positioning around simplicity bias remain substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: There are localized prose revisions, particularly in Sections 5.2 and 8, new appendix sections, and a Metrics/Results subdivision of the plasticity discussion. Affiliations, acknowledgments, conference headers, and cross-references are updated; the main narrative structure and much of the wording remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds component-removal, extended-training, correlation, and component-plasticity displays in Figures 15–17 and 19, and expands the earlier plasticity display into Figure 18. Figure 12 gains an RMSNorm row, and Figure 5 changes its horizontal axis from critic width to parameter count. Existing benchmark tables and learning-curve displays are retained.

improvement.justification: Compared with v1's already broad evaluation, the removal ablations and extended-training tests strengthen evidence about component necessity and performance durability. Acknowledging the RSNorm discrepancy also clarifies the simplicity proxy's limits. These are useful incremental gains, tempered by the unresolved Pearson/Spearman inconsistency in the new correlation analysis.
